new.title: Saturation Level of the Streaming Instability
new.summary: In proto-planetary disks, gas turbulence can cluster dust grains and catalyze the formation of planetesimals. This process depends on the strength of the turbulence. Here, we evaluate the turbulence strength that is induced by the streaming instability. Based on the amount of free energy available, we estimate the viscous parameter to be alpha ~ St Pi^2 f(epsilon), where St (< 1) is the Stokes number of the streaming grains, Pi is the dimensionless pressure gradient, and f (epsilon) is an explicit function of epsilon, the local dust-to-gas density ratio. This estimate explains the results of many previous studies, and is also supported by our additional tailor-made simulations. We discuss two easy applications of our result, one is a self-consistent dust scale height, one is the astrophysical relevance of a pressure bump. Lastly, while this work allows one to characterize the streaming turbulence, we emphasize our current inability to connect the strength of turbulence to the formation of planetesimals.

new.title: Systematic Uncertainties in Rocky Exoplanet Reflected Light from Incomplete Laboratory BRDF Measurements
new.summary: The first observations of short-period rocky exoplanets have initiated the era of terrestrial exoplanet characterization. The interpretation of these observations relies on forward models used in atmospheric and surface retrieval frameworks. While atmospheric modeling is supported by extensive laboratory datasets of molecular opacities, the experimental basis for rocky surface characterization remains limited. Most reflectance libraries of planetary analog materials provide spectra measured at a single illumination and viewing geometry, constraining the spectral behavior but not its full angular scattering properties. We show that incomplete angular coverage in laboratory bidirectional reflectance measurements introduces an intrinsic systematic uncertainty in the interpretation of rocky exoplanet observations. We demonstrate that multiple combinations of photometric parameters can reproduce the same laboratory reflectance spectrum while predicting different angular scattering behaviors and disk-integrated observables. We propagate this non-uniqueness to reflected-light phase curves, geometric albedos, and planet-star contrast ratios between $0.5$--$1.7\,\mu$m, representative of the spectral range targeted by future direct-imaging missions such as the HWO. We find that single-geometry laboratory spectra produce large uncertainties in predicted signals, particularly at small phase angles. Simplified assumptions adopted in exoplanet studies, such as isotropic scattering can additionally introduce systematic biases. Using multi-angular laboratory measurements from the Bloomsburg University Goniometer dataset, we show that the uncertainty in predicted observables collapses once angular scattering behavior is directly constrained. Our results demonstrate that multi-angular measurements are required to construct physically predictive reflected-light models of rocky exoplanets.

new.title: FAUST XXXII. Chemically layered structures and ionisation in the disk and envelope of NGC 1333 IRAS 4C
new.summary: Recent molecular line observations with high spatial resolutions have revealed vertical chemical stratification in Class I/II disks (i.e. chemical composition changing with height in the vertical direction of the disk), as well as a radial variation of ionisation rates. However, such chemical layered structures in Class 0 disk and envelope systems have been investigated only for limited objects, such as L1527. In the context of the ALMA Large Program FAUST, we report the results of molecular line observations toward the disk and envelope around the low-mass Class 0 protostar NGC 1333 IRAS 4C in the Perseus Molecular Cloud. Previous observations have shown that the disk rotation axis of this object is largely tilted to the line of sight, making it suitable for studying the molecular abundance distribution as a function of disk height. We found that the molecules known as gas density tracers such as C18O and H2CO are distributed around the disk midplane. In addition, molecules known as tracers of photochemical reactions such as CCH and c-C3H2 are distributed in the low-density upper layers of the disk, unlike the distribution in L1527. Moreover, the column density ratio of HCO+/CO derived from the H13CO+ and C18O line emission suggests that the ionisation degree and the ionisation rate vary with the disk radius and they are larger in the outer region of the disk and envelope.

new.title: White dwarf pollution in wide binaries I: the effects of stellar evolution
new.summary: Context. Atmospheric pollution in white dwarfs is interpreted as evidence for the accretion of rocky material from remnant planetary systems. Wide binary companions can influence the delivery of planetary material onto white dwarfs, making it essential to understand the interplay between stellar evolution and binary perturbations. Aims. We investigate how uncertainties in stellar mass-loss histories affect the dynamical evolution of remnant planetary systems in wide binaries, and assess their relative importance compared with binary perturbations in driving the accretion of rocky material onto white dwarfs. Methods. We perform REBOUND N-body simulations incorporating time-dependent stellar parameters interpolated from MESA evolutionary tracks and tidal interactions, following the dynamical evolution up to the white dwarf stage. We explore two stellar-evolution models with distinct mass-loss histories for wide binary systems hosting a Jupiter-mass planet and a planetesimal disc, spanning a range of binary architectures. Results. The adopted stellar-evolution model has only a minor effect on the survival of the planet, mainly affecting the timing and efficiency of planetesimal delivery during the white dwarf stage. Instead, the architecture of the binary primarily controls the pollution outcome: wider binaries produce the highest rates of accretion onto the white dwarf, consistent with the observed prevalence of polluted white dwarfs in wide binaries. Moreover, planetesimal reservoirs remain long-lived, with survival times increasing with binary separation, enabling Gyr-long metal pollution. Conclusions. Our results suggest that the architecture of wide binaries, rather than uncertainties in stellar evolution, is the dominant factor controlling the dynamical delivery of rocky material onto white dwarfs.

new.title: Surface regolith model of near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon
new.summary: The near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon displays activity as it comes close to the Sun and is presumed to be the progenitor of the Geminids meteor shower. Both CM- and CY-meteorites have been suggested as possible meteorite analogues for Phaethon. Previous spectral and polarization measurements of Phaethon indicate possible surface heterogeneity in the regolith properties. By combining mineral components and their size fractions, we present a regolith model for Phaethon that reproduces the spectral, polarization, and geometric albedo measurements presented in various studies, with the aim of quantitatively characterizing the surface material and structure, as well as the regolith heterogeneity. The best fit model able to produce the measurements is constructed from large olivine particles with troilite inclusions and small scale surface roughness, mixed with smaller, porous troilite aggregates comprised of monomers resembling interplanetary dust. new.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
new.summary: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

new.title: The morphology of contact binary objects in the Solar System
new.summary: Contact binaries, appearing as two objects stuck together, are prevalent throughout the Solar System, making up between 30- 50% of asteroids and comets. Despite this, detailed shape models of contact binaries are hard to obtain remotely, requiring rare occultation events or close approaches to Earth (< 0.1 au) to observe with ground-based radar systems. Despite only 16 contact binary models being published, there already exists a wide variety of different arrangements of the two lobes relative to one another. At the same time, simulations of contact binary object formation are increasing in scale, producing 10s to 1000s of contact binary candidates per simulation. It is therefore necessary to begin the process of characterising the different shapes observed, and to further investigate any emerging trends. We analyse the size, period, neck prominence, volume distribution, ratio between the sizes and volumes of the individual lobes, and the alignment between them to summarise the extent of the currently modelled asteroids.

new.title: Topographically Forced Stationary Waves Can Explain the Near-Surface Zonal Winds Observed by Huygens on Titan
new.summary: Titan's equatorial superrotation is associated with climatological retrograde (westward) near-surface winds at low latitudes, as consistently simulated by Titan general circulation models. However, the Huygens probe measured prograde (eastward) near-surface winds, contrary to the expected circulation. We investigate whether these observations reflect localized forcing by large-scale topography, using paired three-dimensional dry simulations with and without topography in the Titan Atmospheric Model. We find that topography generates longitude-locked, vertically structured zonal wind anomalies that reproduce key features of the Huygens wind profile in the lowest few kilometers. Helmholtz and spectral analyses show that this structure arises from the superposition of several vertically varying low wavenumber modes. A predominantly rotational, topographically forced stationary zonal wavenumber s=1 response provides a major eastward anomaly throughout the lowest 2 km, whereas a locally divergent s=4 response consistent with a gravity wave, opposes it near the surface. Weaker s=2 and s=3 responses also vary vertically and contribute eastward anomalies near the surface. Combined with the retrograde zonal-mean circulation, these modes produce a Huygens-like profile characterized by prograde flow within the lowest 1 km and shear toward retrograde flow aloft. The paired simulations establish their topographic origin, while coherence with the corresponding terrain-forcing components demonstrates that the responses remain phase locked to the forcing. Similar but weaker stationary responses are simulated near the planned Dragonfly landing site, providing baseline expectations for interpreting its future atmospheric measurements. This study demonstrates how large-scale topography can generate localized departures from Titan's zonal-mean circulation and highlights the importance of stationary waves.

new.title: Predictions for an unseen third planet in the WISPIT 2 system
new.summary: We predict the mass and semi-major axis of a currently unseen but hypothesised planet in the WISPIT 2 system based on the location of the ring observed by ALMA at 144.4 au. Using findings from previous hydrodynamical models, we predict that a ~0.2-1 $M_{Jup}$ planet may exist at ~ 100-120 au. We also discuss how future observations of the system's gas component may help constrain these predictions better, and note that this third planet in WISPIT 2 may be discoverable using upcoming JWST/NIRCam observations or Gaia data release 4 (DR4).

cross.title: Solar System Surface Technosignatures: Searching for Signs of Artificial Design on Extraterrestrial Terrain
cross.summary: Artificial radio emissions have historically been a major focus of technosignature searches. Here, we apply an anthropological lens to expand this scope to surface technosignatures: non-random, intentional patterning on planetary terrain, similar to long-lasting human-made landscapes and monuments on Earth. On geologically inactive bodies such as the Moon and Mars, artificial traces and patterns could potentially remain visible for hundreds of millions of years. We discuss two recent developments that make this search timely: high-resolution imaging datasets, such as those produced by the HiRISE camera on the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), and ML-based anomaly-detection methods. Finally, we list two possible approaches to developing a model capable of searching for these surface technosignatures: a supervised and an unsupervised one. Complemented by LiDAR, ground-penetrating radar, and reflectance spectroscopy, these methods would enable the first quantitative upper limits on surface technosignatures while yielding ancillary benefits for planetary science.

cross.title: The Pandora SmallSat: Target Selection and Early Science
cross.summary: The Pandora spacecraft is a smallsat selected in NASA's inaugural class of Pioneers missions. The aim of the Pandora mission is to disentangle stellar activity signals from exoplanet atmospheric transmission spectroscopy measurements. Pandora accomplishes this goal with its combined visible photometry and NIR spectroscopy that observe each target in the prime mission for 10 separate transit observations, each spanning 24 hours at a time. Targets were carefully selected for the Pandora prime mission. Pandora is specifically studying planets around low-mass stellar hosts (K and M dwarf stars) spanning a range of rotation periods and activity levels. The planets range in size from 1.5 - 15 Earth radii and orbital periods ranging from 1.7 - 11.5 days. In addition to the 10 transit visits planned for each of the 20 prime mission targets, Pandora is observing a number of auxiliary targets encompassing a variety of science topics. This includes topics such as stellar activity and young systems, transit timing variations of exoplanets, brown dwarf compositions, exoplanet phase curves, etc. We will discuss the selection of these targets, how they have been scheduled to fill in gaps in prime mission operations, and early science results. If the mission is extended, there is further opportunity for accomplishing additional science. Here we will discuss the possible options for extended mission operations and science.

repl.summary: We revisit the diffusive instability in dusty disks that arises when the dust mass diffusivity and/or viscosity decreases sufficiently steeply with increasing dust density. Our updated model includes an incompressible, viscous gas that responds azimuthally and couples to the dust through drag. We show that the basic criterion for diffusion-slope-driven instability remains approximately $\beta_\mathrm{diff}\lesssim -2$ for small dust stopping times, with gas feedback providing only modest quantitative changes for parameters motivated by streaming-instability turbulence. We perform nonlinear numerical calculations and confirm linear growth and mode selection toward the fastest-growing wavenumber. However, for power-law closures $D\propto\Sigma^{\beta_\mathrm{diff}}$ with $\beta_\mathrm{diff}<0$, the nonlinear evolution does not saturate. Instead, steepening gradients amplify the nonlinear dust-pressure term and drive finite-time collapse into increasingly sharp spikes. Motivated by the absence of multidimensional saturation channels in our 1D framework, we test a simple piecewise closure in which the negative diffusion slope operates only over a finite density interval. This modification eliminates blowup and produces peak densities controlled by the imposed saturation scale. Our results support diffusive instabilities as a linear organizing mechanism in dusty turbulence, while highlighting that realistic nonlinear saturation requires additional physics beyond the present closure.

repl.title: Analysis of Io's tidal response as a function of the properties of the partially molten layer
repl.summary: Io's internal heat is generated by Jupiter-driven tidal dissipation and Laplace resonance. This energy partially melts the mantle, but the melt fraction, depth, and spatial distribution of dissipation remain poorly constrained. Tidal deformation is linked to the mantle's physical state via a parametric approach accounting for melting onset depth and latent heat of fusion. Io is modeled as a three-layer body comprising a fluid core, a viscoelastic mantle, and an elastic lithosphere. The degree-2 potential Love number k2 is computed by solving spheroidal oscillation equations with an adapted California Planetary Geophysics Code (CPGC). Mantle properties (viscosity, shear modulus, Andrade parameter beta) are iteratively updated based on the local melt fraction, and mantle compressibility is explicitly incorporated. Results show a self-consistent shallow-mantle enhancement of tidal heating. Melt presence decreases effective viscosity and increases anelasticity, amplifying upper-mantle dissipation. Reproducing the observed real part of k2 in 1D models requires melt fractions below the rheologically critical threshold. Compressibility yields higher values for the real part of k2, reinforcing this upper bound. Mass flux analysis confirms melt percolation capacity exceeds thermodynamic production, implying efficient drainage. The reference Andrade parameter beta strongly influences the imaginary Love numbers (k2, h2, l2) and the predicted libration amplitude. These constraints support a heterogeneous mantle characterized by a magmatic sponge structure rather than a global magma ocean, establishing a quantitative framework linking Io's interior, partial melting, and tidal dissipation to Juno observations.

repl.title: A Formation-Stage Bottleneck for Exomoons around Close-in Rocky Planets
repl.summary: Massive moons around rocky exoplanets are expected outcomes of giant impacts, yet no exomoon has been securely confirmed. We address this problem using meshless finite-mass simulations of giant impacts between differentiated rocky planets that include stellar tidal and Coriolis forces in a local co-rotating frame for orbital periods of 1--300 days, and compare these simulations with otherwise identical collisions in isolation. We find that stellar perturbations impose a severe formation-stage bottleneck on moon-forming disks. Ultra-short-period impacts leave essentially no surviving circumplanetary disk, whereas 10-day systems retain only strongly depleted, radially truncated, and dynamically compact disks. High impact velocities, expected for close-in planets, are devastating for disk generation, while retrograde impacts can slightly compensate for disk mass depletion. These results show that stellar perturbations can suppress exomoon formation around close-in rocky planets, reshaping expectations for the demographics of exomoons.

repl.title: Emission spectroscopy of KELT-2A b with Gemini-North/IGRINS-2: hints of a stellar C/O ratio and sub-stellar metallicity
repl.summary: We present the results of high-resolution emission spectroscopy of the hot Jupiter KELT-2A~b using IGRINS-2 on the Gemini-North telescope, covering the $H$- and $K$-bands at a spectral resolution of $R \sim 45{,}000$. Observations were carried out over five nights, covering both pre- and post-eclipse orbital phases. Stellar and telluric contaminations are removed via singular value decomposition. We detect $\rm H_2O$ at a signal-to-noise ratio of {6.57}, confirming the previous result at a higher significance. While $\rm ^{12}CO$ is identified in the log-likelihood map near the expected planetary velocity, a definitive detection of $\rm ^{12}CO$ remains elusive given the current data quality. We perform atmospheric retrieval both with IGRINS-2 data alone and jointly with archival \textit{Spitzer}/IRAC photometric data points. The retrieved temperature--pressure profile is non-inverted, consistent with prior observations. {From the joint fit we constrain the water abundance to} $\rm log(H_2O) = {-3.78^{+0.27}_{-0.20}}$ {with the free chemistry model}. {The chemical equilibrium model yields} $\rm C/O={ 0.19^{+0.12}_{-0.07}}$, $\rm [C/H]=-0.81^{+0.41}_{-0.34}$, and $\rm [O/H] = -0.37^{+0.27}_{-0.17}${: the C/O ratio agrees with the stellar value, while the carbon and oxygen abundances are moderately depleted relative to the host star, though still consistent at the $\sim2\sigma$ level.} If confirmed, {this combination of a stellar C/O ratio with a sub-stellar metallicity is difficult to reconcile with gas accretion between the $\rm{H_2O}$ and CO snowlines, which predicts a super-stellar C/O. It instead points to the accretion of metal-depleted gas outside the CO snowline with only limited planetesimal enrichment, and hence to a disk-free, high-eccentricity migration history.}

repl.title: JOYS: Launch and destruction of dust in protostellar jets. The case of BHR71-IRS1 with JWST MIRI
repl.summary: Protostellar winds can theoretically lift solids from the planet-forming disks, but direct evidence for launched dust has been scarce so far. Numerous atomic lines that are unique to mid-infrared (IR) wavelengths reveal refractories eroded from dust grains and provide information on wind properties in the earliest stages of the star formation process. We present JWST MIRI-MRS spectral imaging of the inner 2000 au of the BHR71-IRS1 blueshifted side of the outflow. Atomic line intensities are compared to shock models to constrain the physical conditions and elemental abundances of the outflowing gas. Dust continuum maps were constructed from PSF-subtracted cubes, and the spectral energy distribution of the dust was analyzed. The ionized central jet of BHR71-IRS1 is spatially resolved and imaged for the first time, revealing a unique inventory of refractory, volatile, and noble-gas fine-structure lines (Fe, Ni, Co, Cl, S, Ne, Ar). The emission is concentrated along four bright knots that wiggle along the jet axis. PSF-subtracted continuum maps reveal extended mid-IR continuum emission co-spatial with the jet bullets and within the H$_2$-traced outflow cone. Spectral energy distributions along the jet are fit together with the extinction, revealing a warm (200-400 K) and a cold (70-90 K) dust component. The shock modeling constrained by the mid-IR lines indicates a decline in the shock velocity from 70 to 35 km s$^{-1}$ and in the pre-shock density from $>$10$^5$ to $ 4\times 10^4$ cm$^{-3}$ with distance from the protostar. Gas-phase Fe and Ni are measurably depleted relative to Solar abundances, consistent with a substantial fraction of refractories remaining locked in grains in spite of the shocks. These JWST observations provide direct evidence that dust is launched in a Class 0 jet and at least partly survives shock processing.

repl.title: Families of relative periodic orbits in the planar three-body problem via consecutive alignments
repl.summary: Relative periodic orbits (RPOs) are solutions of the three-body problem that are periodic in a uniformly rotating reference frame and, in general, quasi-periodic in inertial coordinates. We present a numerical procedure for computing and continuing one-parameter families of RPOs of the planar Newtonian three-body problem. The method exploits consecutive syzygies, understood here as configurations in which the three bodies are aligned and their velocities satisfy the corresponding symmetry conditions. Matching the positions and momenta at two consecutive alignments reduces the computation of RPOs to a low-dimensional nonlinear problem. Its solutions are then numerically continued, and linear stability is determined from the nontrivial eigenvalues of the rotated monodromy matrix after removing the neutral directions associated with conserved quantities and continuous symmetries. The procedure is applied to several mass distributions and initial configurations, producing families of Poincaré, Hill, and binary-type solutions. These families exhibit transitions from nearly circular to highly eccentric motion, changes of stability near resonances and turning points, and absolute periodic solutions when the rotation angle is a rational multiple of 2{\pi}. In the Hill families, the continuation connects satellite configurations with circumstellar motion as the smallest body loses its gravitational binding to the intermediate body. Circumbinary and circumstellar configurations are also obtained in the binary regime. The results illustrate the dynamical diversity of RPOs and provide coherent three-body motions that can be used as prescribed trajectories in restricted four-body models.

repl.title: A Solar Optical Clock
repl.summary: Precision spectroscopy underpins quantum sensing, atomic timekeeping, and the search for terrestrial-mass exoplanets. Finding an Earth-Sun analog requires fractional splitting of spectral features that rivals the precision of the best laboratory spectroscopy. This corresponds to resolution of a few parts in $10^5$ of a typical stellar spectral line, or a Doppler velocity precision of less than 10 cm s$^{-1}$. Only a few astrophysical spectrometers reach this regime, and only by dispersing starlight with large gratings and averaging thousands of lines. Here, we show that comparable precision can be achieved on a single solar line by leveraging techniques used in quantum sensors and optical clocks. A laser is frequency-locked to the 1565 nm solar Fe I line by coupling to a single mode of the solar thermal field and counted against an optical frequency comb referenced to the SI second, thus creating a solar optical clock. Operating at the fundamental photon-noise limit of thermal heterodyne spectroscopy, we achieve centroid precision of one part in $10^9$ of the optical frequency, or 30 cm s$^{-1}$ in radial velocity. We recover the Sun's five-minute acoustic oscillations and the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signal during a solar eclipse. Combining these techniques from quantum sensing with a thirty-meter-class telescope could enable our demonstrated precision on the nearest Sun-like stars in a few hours. Multiplexing such absolute frequency measurements across lines with different magnetic sensitivity and formation depth would reduce averaging time and help disentangle stellar granulation and activity from the Doppler signature of terrestrial exoplanets, providing new approaches to address some of the most demanding measurements in astrophysical spectroscopy.

(b) Schematic of a solar optical clock. A probe laser is locked to the center of a transition in the solar spectrum using heterodyne spectroscopy and modulation techniques. The frequency of the probe laser is simultaneously measured relative to an optical frequency comb. A loop filter locks the LO to the zero crossing, and the frequency of the stabilized LO laser is simultaneously measured against an optical frequency comb.

A small drift is present due to coupling between the apparent orientation of the Sun’s rotational axis and a slight asymmetry in the antenna pattern of the light collection optics. Binning of the FM data to 100 s intervals yields the smoothed grey line. (b) The power spectral density (PSD) of these binned data clearly reveals the 5.5 min oscillation period characteristic of solar p-modes. (c) The Allan deviations of the FM and swept LHR data. Again, evidence of solar p-modes is present for the FM data, which shows a peak in the averaging time at half the p-mode period ( ∼ \sim 150 s). The dotted lines represent the Allan deviation after linearly detrending the frequency shifts, and the dashed line indicates the theoretical quantum-limit for FM-locked LHR sensitivity discussed in Section 3 and derived analytically in the Appendix.

figures.caption: Simultaneous FM-locked and swept LHR data taken during the 2024 solar eclipse in Boulder CO, USA. (a) Optical frequency shifts measured during the eclipse, which clearly show the expected Rossiter-McLaughlin signature produced by the partial occultation of the solar disk. (b) Detrended frequency shifts between the swept and FM-locked measurements, illustrating the relative scatter between the two approaches. (c) Five-second Allan deviation for the FM-locked and swept measurements plotted as a function of time during the eclipse. Also shown is the independently measured solar irradiance which decreases during the eclipse, thereby increasing the frequency scatter and Allan deviation.
